problem: The sentence 'NPSHR rises with flow and speed, so a pump that is safe at design flow may cavitate when throttled or run faster' contradicts itself and the rest of the chapter. Throttling the discharge reduces flow, so NPSHR falls; the chapter's own Q8 correctly says cavitation risk grows at higher flow. As written, a student will think closing the delivery valve causes cavitation.
fix: Write: 'NPSHR rises with flow and with speed. A pump that is safe at design flow may cavitate if it is run at a higher flow than design (for example with the discharge valve fully open on a steep system curve) or at a higher speed. Throttling the discharge reduces flow and usually reduces NPSHR, though running far below design flow brings its own problems such as recirculation.'

problem: The standard textbook definition is that the Thoma cavitation factor σ is NPSHA/H, and its critical value σ_c (at which cavitation begins) is NPSHR/H. Presenting only σ = NPSHR/H labels the critical value with the plain name.
fix: Write: 'Some texts define the Thoma cavitation factor σ = NPSH_A/H, with a critical value σ_c = NPSH_R/H at which cavitation begins; σ is a maker's index, not a replacement for the NPSH comparison.'

problem: 'The second is the head spent in boiling the liquid' is misleading. p_v/(ρg) is the head equivalent of the vapour pressure, that is, the absolute pressure at which the liquid boils at that temperature; nothing is 'spent' in boiling.
fix: Write: 'The second is the vapour pressure head — the absolute pressure at which the liquid boils at its temperature — which must be subtracted because it is unavailable as suction margin.'

problem: Saying NPSHR is the NPSHA at which the maker 'guarantees cavitation-free operation' is too strong. By standard test practice it is the NPSH at which the pump head has dropped by a fixed small amount (commonly 3%) from the cavitation-free value, so it already contains an acceptance margin, not a zero-cavitation guarantee.
fix: Write: 'NPSH required is the NPSH at which the pump head falls by a stated small amount (commonly 3%) in the maker's test, taken as the onset of cavitation; it already includes the eye and inlet losses of that pump.'
